text: Imagine having thousands of legal documents, statutes, and court judgments, but still needing to search through them every time you want to answer a legal question.
That is the problem we set out to solve with Indian Law GPT.
In this video, I'll explain what we built, why we built it, how it works, what we tested, and what we learned.
We wanted to create an AI-powered legal research assistant that could help users find relevant information from Indian legal documents and generate answers grounded in that information.
But we did not want to build just another chatbot that produces convincing sounding legal answers.
Legal research requires finding the right provisions, identifying relevant judgments, connecting answers to their sources, and checking whether the evidence actually supports what the AI says.
That is why our focus was on building an evidence-based research system with retrieval and citation verification at its core.
We also wanted to experiment with adapting a smaller, locally running language model and compare its performance against other models.
We built Indian Law GPT with four main components, a legal document collection, a retrieval system, an answer generation system, and a citation verification system.
We also built a research interface where users can ask questions, inspect citations, open documents, and compare answers from different models.
The foundation of the system is our legal data. According to our project report, the corpus contains 38,432 documents and 64,651 indexed passages.
It includes 38,238 statutory sections, 832 central acts, and 194 judgments.
We organized this information so the system could retrieve relevant passages rather than relying only on the language model's general knowledge.
Our statutory collection is broad, while our case law collection is more focused, with particular concentration on section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
We made this distinction because having a large collection of documents does not automatically mean that every area of Indian law is covered.
Once we had the data, we needed a way to find the right information.
A simple keyword search can miss relevant passages when a user asks a question using different wording.
Semantic search can help find passages with similar meaning, but legal research also requires exact references, section numbers, and connections between older and newer laws.
So we developed a hybrid retrieval system. It combines semantic search, keyword search using BM25, explicit legal reference matching, old law to new law mapping, and case law retrieval.
We combine these results using a ranking method called reciprocal rank fusion.
In simple terms, we use multiple ways to search for relevant legal information and combine their results into one ranked list.
We did this because we wanted to improve the system's ability to find the specific sources required by a legal question.
In one held out evaluation, the system retrieved 106 out of 112 required sources, giving a retrieval rate of 94.6%.
This measures source retrieval on that evaluation set, not the correctness of every answer.
Finding a relevant document is only one part of legal research. A model might produce a citation that looks correct but points to the wrong source.
It might also provide a quotation that does not appear in the retrieved document.
We wanted to reduce that risk so we built citation verification into the pipeline.
The model proposes quotations as supporting evidence.
Our Python code then checks whether those quotations can be matched against the retrieved text.
When a quotation matches, the system connects it to the actual source metadata.
When it does not match, it can be marked as unverified.
We also avoid simply trusting a document identifier supplied by the model.
The source is mapped using the retrieved evidence and it stored metadata.
We built this because we wanted users to inspect the evidence behind an answer instead of having to trust the model blindly.
However, verifying that a quotation exists does not prove that the legal interpretation is correct or that a provision applies to every situation.
Next, we developed the research application. The front end uses React, Vite and TypeScript, while fast API powers the backend.
When a user submits a question, the interface can show the research progress including searching, ranking, drafting and verification.
The answer is displayed with numbered citations and an evidence panel.
Users can open-sided documents in a reader where relevant passages can be highlighted.
We also built statute and case law search along with a comparison feature for older and newer legal codes such as IPC and BNS.
CRPC and BNSS and the Evidence Act and BSA.
We included browser local research history so previous research can be revisited.
We built these features because we wanted users to do more than read an AI-generated response.
We wanted them to explore the sources and understand how the answer was produced.
After building the retrieval and answer pipeline, we wanted to investigate another possibility.
Could we adapt a smaller local language model to follow the answering style
and structured output of our legal research system?
This is where fine-tuning and knowledge distillation became part of the project.
Rag retrieves information from a knowledge base when a question is asked.
Fine-tuning updates and models weights using training examples.
Our goal was to explore whether carefully reviewed examples could help a smaller model
produce more useful legal research responses.
We did not assume that fine-tuning would automatically make the model legally correct.
We wanted to test it. Before training, we needed reliable examples.
We built a pipeline for generating questions, checking their answer ability,
producing teacher answers, and reviewing those answers.
The question generation process checked whether seed sources existed and whether
proposed evidence quotations appeared in retrieved passages.
An independent cloud reviewer assessed questions for answerability, ambiguity, and quality.
Teacher answers were generated through our existing answer pipeline and then passed through
deterministic checks in an independent grading process.
Examples were assigned statuses such as verified, needs review, or rejected.
We did this because training on incorrect or poorly supported answers could teach the model
those same mistakes. We wanted a quality control process before scaling up the dataset.
Our first completed Laura experiment was deliberately small.
We selected 30 verified teacher answers and used them to train a Laura adapter on
Quinn 3-1.7b. We used 4-bit quantization and MLX on Apple Silicon.
After training, we compared three answer engines, the original Quinn model,
the fine-tuned Quinn model, and Claude.
All three answered the same 50 held out questions using identical retrieved evidence.
We used the same evidence because we wanted to compare how the models generated answers
without allowing different retrieval results to influence the comparison.
We evaluated legal correctness, evidence support, citation accuracy, structured output,
hallucinated facts, and response time.
The purpose was to understand what fine-tuning had actually improved and where it had caused problems.
The results were mixed and that was an important learning experience.
The fine-tuned model improved some aspects of citation behavior and structured output.
For example, 31 out of 50 responses met our citation accuracy criterion
compared with zero for the base Quinn model in this test.
However, the legal correctness results were worse.
The base Quinn model produced 15 fully correct answers out of 50
while the fine-tuned model produced six.
The fine-tuned model also had problems with malformed or truncated responses.
So, although its overall blended score increased,
that increase did not represent an improvement in legal correctness,
we classified the pilot as a regression requiring further investigation,
and we did not scale it.
This taught us that better formatting and citation behavior
do not necessarily mean better legal reasoning.
We then integrated the three answer engines into the application,
Claude, Plain Quinn, running through Olima, and the experimental Laura Quinn model.
The system retrieves evidence once and freezes it into an evidence bundle.
Each selected engine then answers using that same evidence.
This allows us to compare their responses side by side.
Each answer has its own citation panel, evidence drawer, and model details.
We also added structured output status checks so malformed,
truncated, or failed responses are visible rather than silently hidden.
We built this comparison environment because we wanted to evaluate model behavior
using a consistent set of evidence and make the differences easier to inspect.
The fine-tuned model remains experimental.
Its presence in the application is for comparison and investigation,
not proof that it is better.
We also worked on making the prototype understandable and demonstrable.
We added a citation check panel showing proposed, matched, and rejected quotations.
We added an evidence panel showing document identifiers,
pages, sections, and retrieval information.
We made the corpus metrics and architecture visible in the application.
We also prepared curated questions that the current corpus could answer,
along with a deliberately unanswerable question to demonstrate the importance of insufficient evidence.
We tested the application through evaluation runs and a scripted browser walkthrough.
We pushed the project to GitHub while keeping sensitive keys,
local databases, model artifacts, and training data out of the repository.
So where does Indian LogyPT stand today?
The rag pipeline and citation verification system are live and evaluated.
The research interface supports Claude, Plainquen, and the experimental Laura Quen model.
The retrieval improvements have been tested against several evaluation sets,
and the three-engine interface has been demonstrated locally.
However, the larger training data generation runs were stopped before teacher answers were completed.
The 30-example Laura pilot was completed, but it did not demonstrate improved legal correctness,
so we did not scale it.
The broader three-engine benchmark was also paused before completion.
There is another important limitation.
Hosting the front end alone does not host the back end, legal database,
Olama runtime, or MLX model service.
So the current project is a demo-ready, legal research prototype,
not a fully deployed production grade legal service.
Building Indian Law GPT has involved much more than connecting a language model to a collection of documents.
We organized legal data, improved retrieval, verified citations, designed an application,
prepared training examples, and evaluated model behavior.
We also learned that a model can improve in one area while getting worse in another.
Our fine-tuning experiment showed why it is important to evaluate legal correctness separately
from formatting and citation performance.
The next step is to investigate the fine-tuning regression,
improve the quality of training examples, and continue testing before scaling the model adaptation work.
Ultimately, our goal is to build a legal research system where users can inspect the evidence,
understand the limitations, and evaluate the answers rather than simply accepting what an AI says.
That is Indian Law GPT, an evidence-grounded legal research prototype,
a platform for comparing different answer engines, and a foundation for further experimentation with legal AI.
Thank you for watching.
